stories.headline: Trump continues midterm campaign blitz in Mississippi amid outcry over racist, Islamophobic attacks – as it happened
stories.claim: Trump campaigned in Mississippi for Cindy Hyde-Smith, dismissing critics and recirculating polling clips that omit key context.
stories.summary: Donald Trump held a midterm rally in Corinth, Mississippi, backing Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith against Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom. He claimed his rallies had changed the midterm debate and repeated claims of a golden age of prosperity, without mentioning high inflation and petrol prices. A protester interrupted the speech over his White House ballroom. The rally also featured CNN polling clips that, according to the live blog, omitted Harry Enten's caveats about non-Maga Republican support falling sharply. The day's coverage also covered the charging of James Comey and Trump's remarks on Lula's Brazilian election win.
key_points: Trump held a rally in Corinth, Mississippi, supporting Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.
He argued that his campaigning would reverse the usual midterm pattern against sitting presidents.
He did not mention high inflation and petrol prices, which the report links to his tariffs and the Iran war.
A protester was removed after shouting about the White House ballroom during the speech.
The live blog says clips shown at the rally omitted context about falling support among non-Maga Republicans.
stories.market_take: Midterm politics may influence US policy expectations, but this rally itself is unlikely to move markets.

stories.headline: Down Drives Fashion’s Animal Material Shift, Four Paws Finds
stories.claim: Four Paws report finds only 8% of brands using animal-derived materials have taken steps to reduce them.
stories.summary: Animal welfare group Four Paws published its Animal Welfare in Fashion 2026 report, assessing 332 brands in its Wear It Kind Directory. Only 26 of 321 brands using animal-derived materials, or 8%, had committed to reducing that use, with most commitments focused on replacing virgin down. The report found that 14% had eliminated virgin down or gone beyond certification on live plucking, and that 82% of brands prohibit fur. Four Paws also raised concerns that certification audits do not consistently cover parent farms, and that most brands do not disclose virgin down volumes.
key_points: 26 of 321 brands using animal-derived materials had committed to reducing their use, about 8%.
Replacing virgin down accounted for 85% of reduction commitments identified.
Dior, Fendi and Louis Vuitton were rated among the lowest luxury brands for continued fur use; Stella McCartney, Another Tomorrow and Chloé led on fur.
Only 20% of the 318 wool-using brands source exclusively certified mulesing-free wool.
Four Paws wants mandatory audits covering parent farms, fattening farms and slaughterhouses; the assessment cutoff was 31 July 2026.

stories.headline: Over 11 million bitcoin has no known owner. Here's what it means
stories.claim: Galaxy's October data shows about 55% of bitcoin supply sits in wallets with no known owner.
stories.summary: Research firm Galaxy's October snapshot classifies about 11.1 million BTC, roughly 55% of supply, as unattributed to any known owner. Galaxy's head of research, Alex Thorn, argues this suggests self-custody by individuals remains widespread, despite growth in exchanges, funds and institutional custodians. Xapo Bank responded that the large unnamed holdings show retail investors have been involved for over a decade. The article notes the unattributed coins may include lost coins, institutional holdings Galaxy has not identified, and coins spread across custody setups. The 45% with names attached includes exchanges, BlackRock-led ETFs, the US government and the Satoshi-era miner pattern holding about 1.12 million BTC.

stories.headline: ‘Rent in advance’ ban causes problems for many tenants
stories.claim: Letting agency bosses at LRG and Connells say the Renters' Rights Act ban on rent-in-advance is hurting poorer and overseas tenants.
stories.summary: Two large UK estate agency groups, LRG and Connells, have told the Government that the recent ban on landlords and letting agents requesting rent in advance is causing problems. Connells chief executive Helen Charlesworth described a nurse with a poor credit rating who, unable to pay rent up front, could not secure another tenancy after a Section 21 eviction. LRG's Allison Thompson said the ban has hit international students, who previously offered several months' rent in advance, and suggested guarantors as a workaround. Both say they support the overall aims of the Renters' Rights Act but argue the ban has had unintended effects that the industry predicted. The firms say they are passing these examples to government contacts.

Connells' chief executive Helen Charlesworth cited a nurse with a poor credit rating who was left without a home.

With Section 21 gone, landlords are less willing to take risks on tenants, the agencies say.

The agencies are raising the issue with government contacts, but no policy change has been announced.

stories.headline: Nearly 2,000 Boeing 737s Must Get Tail Inspections After Jets Pitched Up And Down Mid-Flight
stories.claim: FAA orders tail inspections on nearly 2,000 US-registered Boeing 737NG jets over horizontal stabilizer freeplay.
stories.summary: The US Federal Aviation Administration has issued an airworthiness directive requiring inspections of 1,987 US-registered Boeing 737NG aircraft. The checks look for excessive freeplay in the horizontal stabilizer hinges and jackscrew, which could lead to flutter and loss of control if not fixed. The directive takes effect on 23 November and follows several reports of pitch oscillation events, though the FAA did not give details of the incidents. Airlines including United and Alaska asked for more time or flexibility, but the FAA rejected those requests. Each inspection is estimated to cost about $510 per aircraft, with more than $1 million across the US fleet, excluding parts.

stories.summary: Huawei has officially confirmed the Pura 90 Plus and opened pre-orders in China ahead of a 28 October launch. Live images from retail displays show a Kirin 9025 chipset, 12GB of RAM, a 2848x1276 screen, HarmonyOS 7 and the LCI-AL00 model number. Tipsters claim the phone offers a 19% overall performance gain over the Pura 80 Pro and performs on par with the Kirin 9030S. Reported specs include a 6.8-inch curved 1.5K LTPO OLED display, 120Hz refresh and a 50MP 1-inch main camera with variable aperture. Pricing will be revealed at the launch event, and benchmarks are still needed to verify performance claims.
key_points: Huawei has confirmed the Pura 90 Plus and opened pre-orders in China.
The phone launches on 28 October 2026, when pricing will be revealed.
Live images show the Kirin 9025 chipset, 12GB RAM and HarmonyOS 7.
Tipsters claim a 19% performance gain over the Pura 80 Pro, but this is unverified.

stories.headline: On a Paris Island, an Art Museum Finally Takes Shape
stories.claim: Le Large, a new contemporary art centre on Île Seguin near Paris, has opened in the former Renault factory site.
stories.summary: Le Large, a 53,800 square foot contemporary art centre funded by the Emerige group's founder Laurent Dumas, has opened on Île Seguin, an island on the Seine near Paris. The building was designed by the Pritzker Prize-winning firm RCR Arquitectes, and Emerige has spent about 200 million euros on the wider Pointe des Arts district. Nearly half the museum is free to enter. The inaugural exhibition, Imaginary Engine, curated by Cecilia Alemani, explores car culture and the industrial legacy of the Renault factory, and includes works from Renault's art fund. The site was once planned by François Pinault, who abandoned his plans more than 20 years ago.
key_points: Le Large opened on Île Seguin, the former Renault factory island on the Seine in Boulogne-Billancourt.
Designed by RCR Arquitectes; Emerige has spent about 200 million euros on the wider cultural district.
Nearly half the museum is free to visit and it will host two major exhibitions a year.
The opening exhibition, Imaginary Engine, is curated by Cecilia Alemani and features 17 new commissions.
Local officials have approved transport improvements, including the Grand Paris Express, due from next year.

stories.headline: Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege
stories.claim: A Houthi siege of Taiz is pushing the city's hospitals, including dialysis services, towards collapse.
stories.summary: Hospitals in the government-held city of Taiz, Yemen, are warning of collapse because of a renewed Houthi siege that began in early October. The Republican Hospital's dialysis centre, which treats 270 patients, has cut sessions from four hours to two and a half and may shut within days. Diesel and medical supplies are critically low, with diesel bought on the black market at five times its earlier price. The WHO has warned that 42 health facilities in Taiz city report severe shortages, and Amnesty International has called for roads to be reopened. Across the governorate, around 1,110 kidney failure patients are at risk.
key_points: A renewed Houthi siege of Taiz began in early October after Houthi advances in the countryside.
The Republican Hospital's dialysis centre, with 270 patients, has cut sessions and may close within days.
The WHO reports 42 health facilities in Taiz city face severe shortages of fuel, oxygen and medicines.
Diesel prices on the black market have reached five times their pre-siege level.
Amnesty International and the UN have called on the Houthis to lift restrictions on supplies.

stories.headline: How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
stories.claim: Analysis of how Benjamin Netanyahu has reshaped Israel's institutions ahead of the October 27 election.
stories.summary: Al Jazeera examines Benjamin Netanyahu's long career as Israel's longest-serving prime minister, ahead of the October 27 election in which he seeks re-election. The piece argues his most enduring domestic legacy may be the right-wing, militaristic opposition he helped create. It details his influence over religious courts, the 2018 Nation-State Basic Law, judicial selection changes and his dismissal of the military advocate general. It also notes his corruption cases, which he denies, and the ICC warrant against him, and says his opponents want to reverse his changes.
key_points: Netanyahu, born in 1949, is Israel's longest-serving prime minister and seeks re-election on October 27.
Analysts say his lasting domestic legacy may be the right-wing opposition he helped create.
His government expanded religious court powers and funding for ultra-Orthodox institutions.
Changes to the Judicial Selection Committee aimed to increase political influence over judges, which critics called a coup.
He faces three corruption cases from 2019, which he denies, and an ICC warrant over Gaza, according to the article.
Opponents pledge to reverse his changes, though analysts say this may be difficult.

stories.headline: US Election Angst Looms for Stocks and the AI Boom
stories.claim: Wall Street expects stocks may fall if Democrats win Congress, but the reality is more nuanced given Trump's veto.
stories.summary: Bloomberg looks at how the US midterm election, less than two weeks away, could affect stocks and the AI boom. The conventional view is that equities fall if Democrats take both houses of Congress. Bloomberg argues the picture is more nuanced. Democrats are seen as more likely to back AI regulation that could slow the sector. However, Donald Trump would still hold a veto, and Democrats are unlikely to reach the two-thirds majority needed to override it, which limits their ability to pass tax rises or rules markets dislike.
key_points: The midterm election is less than two weeks away.
Wall Street generally expects stocks to fall if Democrats win both houses of Congress.
Democrats are seen as more likely to back regulation that could slow the AI boom.
Trump's veto would limit Democrats' ability to enact tax rises or regulation.

Bloomberg has published an explainer on the topic.
stories.market_take: Investors may watch the midterm outcome for AI-linked and regulation-sensitive stocks, though the effect is seen as more nuanced than a simple sell-off.

stories.headline: Intel Tech Chief Says It Is Only A Few Percent Behind TSMC On Performance, But Catching Up In Scale Will Be Slow – VP Asserts High NA EUV Is The Right Choice
stories.claim: Intel executives say its process is only a few percent behind TSMC on performance and that catching up on scale will be slow.
stories.summary: Intel's manufacturing chief Chris Auth and CTO Pushkar Ranade spoke on the Dwarkesh podcast about Intel's position against TSMC. Auth argued that Intel's backside power delivery lets it print circuits directly with High NA EUV lithography, whereas TSMC needs double patterning. He said 14A is available in the process design kit and is being handled customer by customer. Ranade conceded TSMC is a much larger wafer maker but said Intel is already close on technology, perhaps a few percent behind on performance, power or density, and that execution and yield matter most.
key_points: Intel says backside power delivery lets it use High NA EUV in a single pass, avoiding the double patterning TSMC uses.
Auth says 14A is an option in the process design kit and is being discussed with customers individually.
CTO Pushkar Ranade admits TSMC is far larger in wafer output and that catching up on scale will be slow.
Ranade says Intel is only a few percent behind on performance, power or density, and stresses on-time execution and high yields.
Supply chain reports reportedly suggest TSMC is accelerating its own production timeline.
The executives also discussed stacked transistor research, which IBM has announced for a 0.7nm node.
stories.market_take: Comments reinforce Intel's foundry pitch, which may matter to investors watching its 14A customer wins, though the impact is modest.

stocks.reason: Executives push its foundry credibility, but they concede scale gap versus TSMC.
